Asahel
AS-ah-hel
n. (the youngest son of Zeruiah, brother of Joab and Abishai, one of David's thirty)
Hebrew Asahel, God hath made, or made of God, from asah, to make or do, and El, God; borne by several men, chiefly David's nephew, 2 Samuel 2:18.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Asahel was the youngest of David's three warrior nephews, and Scripture introduces him by the gift that killed him: “And there were three sons of Zeruiah there, Joab, and Abishai, and Asahel: and Asahel was as light of foot as a wild roe” (2 Samuel 2:18). At the pool of Gibeon he outran Abner and would not be waved off; Abner warned him three times and then struck: “Howbeit he refused to turn aside: wherefore Abner with the hinder end of the spear smote him under the fifth rib, that the spear came out behind him; and he fell down there, and died in the same place: and it came to pass, that as many as came to the place where Asahel fell down and died stood still” (2 Samuel 2:23). The death set a blood feud running that cost Abner his life under a flag of truce: “And when Abner was returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside in the gate to speak with him quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother” (2 Samuel 3:27). He is nevertheless numbered with the best men in Israel: “Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem” (2 Samuel 23:24). Several later Levites bear the name; this Asahel is the one the narrative follows.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Asahel, God hath made; the youngest son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab, swift of foot, slain by Abner at Gibeon; also the name of several Levites.

Hebrew Asahel, God hath made, or made of God.

From asah, to make or do, compounded with El, God.

The chief bearer was the youngest son of Zeruiah, David's sister.

He was swift of foot, one of the thirty, and was slain by Abner at Gibeon.

Levites of the same name served under Jehoshaphat and Hezekiah.

Modern Corruption

Courage is celebrated as its own virtue; Asahel's refusal to turn aside was courage without judgment, and it cost him his life and Abner his.

expand to see more

A culture that prizes boldness as an unqualified good has nothing to say about Asahel except that he was brave. The narrative is more careful. He was the fastest man in the army and he used it to run down the most dangerous soldier in Israel alone; Abner, who did not want the blood of Joab's brother on him, told him three times to take another man's armour instead and turn aside. He refused to turn aside, and the text pauses on the men who stopped where he fell. Valour without counsel is how young men die.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the long reach of blood vengeance, and why God took it out of private hands. Asahel's death gave Joab a grievance he nursed until he could murder Abner in a city gate under a truce, which David cursed and which Solomon finally avenged. The law's cities of refuge and its requirement of witnesses and judges exist precisely because a brother's blood, left to a brother, never stops.

Hebrew Asahel, God hath made, or made of God.

From asah, to make, with El, God.

The youngest of the three sons of Zeruiah, David's sister.

Swift of foot, numbered among David's thirty, slain by Abner at Gibeon.

Borne also by Levites under Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and in the days of Ezra.
